Homage to Mañjuvajra!
Having first prostrated to Mañjuvajra and immediately thereafter to the feet of the Protector, this method of non-mental engagement, which brings about great exaltation, shall be explained. (1)
The Perfectly Awakened Ones and the Bodhisattvas, as well as the Siddhas instructed by them,
[and] those who have been consecrated as Perfectly Awakened Ones— such is held to be the sequence of their tradition. (2)
There, at the beginning of this turning of the wheel of Dharma, the Blessed One, surrounded by his disciples,
attended upon by those disciples, taught the perfections and so forth.
Then, having completely abandoned him, he went to the southern region;
there, having fashioned that most beautiful maṇḍala called the Dharmadhātu, (4)
The Lord Dhātvākṣa himself and the sixteen bodhisattvas are present here.
There were eight leaders and likewise eight sub-leaders;
they are named in order as they are situated within the mandala.
This maṇḍala, taught by the Guru, is consistent with the tradition. Maitreya, Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, and Khagarbha—
And Lokeśvara, Mañjuśrī, as well as Sarvanivāraṇa; (7) Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Candrābha, Sūryābha, and Amalakīrti.
Samantabhadra, Śūnyābha, Vimalaprabha, as well as Dharmodgata, Ratnamati, and Vyomagañja, and Sudhana— these are situated in the maṇḍala in due order. (8)
Then Sudhana, having bestowed upon them the consecration and [the teachings on] the perfections and so forth—
[the teachings on] the perfections and so forth—
Having been entrusted by the Lion of the Śākyas, he was prophesied by him [the Buddha]:
"This one shall become the noble Nāgārjuna, possessed of great intelligence;
by him also, the turning of the wheel of Dharma must be set in motion."
In this city of Karahāṭaka, in this region of the Southern Path (Dakṣiṇāpatha), [I have taught] the Dharma.
He was born into a brahmin family; his father was Trivikrama and his mother was named Sāvitrī. This is another opinion from the prophecy:
her name was Sāvitrī.
Renowned as Dāmodara while in the state of a mendicant, he bore another name, Śākyamitraka; he remained intent upon the act of bestowing grace upon Ratnamati.
(12) Ratnamati.

Because Saraha was empowered by Vajrayoginī as "the non-dual Vajra" (*advayavajra*), he attained accomplishment (*siddhi*); through her grace, he became her benefactor, and by her favor, that name was bestowed upon him. (13–14)
First he performed that [rite],
and then he heard of Hayagrīva as being beyond perception.
Together with Ratnamati, he set out again for Varendrī; having had a likeness of the wise Bodhisattva fashioned, (15) he [placed it] there.
Having performed worship to him every day, Nāgārjuna dwelt in a secluded place in the village of Purākhya, well-composed in meditation. (16) % pūjā \ms grāme deśe purākhye tu ekāntaḥ susamāhitaḥ
In the city called Daiḍhyapura, there was a dancer named Loka, and his fellow practitioner was Gaurā. (17) [Note:
*sahacāriṇī* is glossed in the manuscript as *naṭī* (actress).]
Their son was Triśaraṇa; among the noble ones, he showed them both that supreme Ratnamati. He said to him: "Do you not see?"
[O Ratnamati: "How can you, being yourself deficient, perceive in an instant that son of an actor named Advayavajra, who is [himself] a moment of gnosis? (18)
In that moment, being impaired, Triśaraṇa replied to him: "Therefore, grant me your favor. [The reference is to Nāgārjuna.]
O son of an actor,
as I see that Protector with the eye of primordial wisdom that transcends the senses—
just so [I see him] in the midst of the noble ones.
Having obtained the authorization of the noble Nāgārjuna, he then became a siddha; and thereafter he was truly favored by the Bodhisattva Triśaraṇa according to the reality of the matter. (20)
By the Bodhisattva Ratnamati,
the place of practice— the breaking of the mind and the resting of the mind— has been discerned.
Assuming the form of a Śabara, he dwelt there.
"He is a Śabara!
Thus ends the tradition known as the *Buddhabodhisattvasiddhāmnāya*.

Indrabhūtipā; Uḍḍiyānavinī Vajrayoginī; Tilopā; Nāropā; Advayavajrapā; Dhyāyīpā; the great paṇḍita Amoghaśrī; or alternatively, Śabaranātha; Advayavajra; Vajrapāṇi; Paiṇḍapātika; the paṇḍita Abhayakaragupta; and again, [the lineage] of Advayavajra.
The etymological derivation and purification (*nirukti-viśuddhi*) of Vajravārāhī:
*vaḥ* is compassion, the wheel of skillful means (*upāya-cakra*); *jaḥ* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The single letter *repha* (*ra*) is the union of these two.
External, beyond speech, its form devoid of the letters *ra* and *ā*,
it transcends the nature of words.
The non-perception of causes is the syllable *hī*, Vārāhī preceded by Vajra; this is purification in the ultimate sense.
Through the purification of body, speech, and mind, there is the triangle.
Because there is no distinction between cause and fruit, the triangle is the equality known as the source of phenomena (dharmodayā).
Homage to the illustrious Vajrayoginī.

First, perform the external worship with vermilion (*sindūra*); if that is unavailable, do so with the mantra. Having drawn [the deity] in by means of the rays of the syllable *hūṃ* situated upon the sun within one’s own heart, and having caused [them] to enter, worship [her] thoroughly with flowers and other offerings. Immediately thereafter, having rendered the world empty (*śūnyīkṛtya*), and following that emptiness, one should instantly visualize oneself as the Blessed Lady (*Bhagavatī*). Upon the summit of a mountain, endowed with various flowers, one should emanate the rays of the syllable *hūṃ* situated upon the sun; this yoga is like the reflection in a mirror through the breath of one's own inhalation. Upon the summit of the mountain... the rays of the syllable *hūṃ*.

While meditating on the mountain and so forth as being like a foot-ointment during the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), one should drink [the nectar] through the left nostril. One should perform the visualization of the offering (*balibhāvanā*) three times a day. Just as the sun, independent of [the state of] a child or a youth, ascends the mountain with its own rays, so too should one visualize the Blessed Lady as having ascended the mountain. One should taste the nectar. For the sake of bestowing accomplishment (*siddhi*), having inscribed the mantra upon the tongue, one should cause [the disciple] to enter by means of the resonance (*nāda*) of the light-rays from one's own heart.
[This is for] the Blessed Lady; [in the case of] bestowing grace upon disciples, [it is performed] as follows.

The Lineage of Gurus of Vajrayoginī: Śavarapa; Sāgaradatta; Vijayaghoṣa; Anaṅgavajra; Biso; Paiṇḍapātika; Paṇḍita Vinayagupta; Mahāpaṇḍita Vāgīśvara; Avadhūta Sudhanaśrī; Līlāvajra; Lalitavajra; the venerable scholars of the monastery.
Homage to the Omniscient One! Homage to the glorious Lord of the Śavaras!

In this very Middle Country, near the great city of Kapilavastu, there was a small village named Jhātakaraṇī. In that place lived a woman of the brahmin caste named Nānukā and a brahmin woman named Sādhvī. Then, after some time had passed...

His son was named Dāmodara. When that prince, about eleven years of age, had mastered half of the *Sāman* Veda, he departed from his home and became a single-staffed ascetic named Martabodha. Subsequently, while residing there, he heard the *Pāṇini-vyākaraṇa*.

Having mastered all the treatises by the age of seven, he studied logic, the inner sciences, the Pāramitānaya, and other scriptures for twenty years in the presence of the venerable Nāropa. Subsequently, he resided together with Rāgavajra, who was an expert in the scriptures of the Mantranaya.

For a period of five years; thereafter, for one year, he studied the system of formlessness (*nirākāra-vyavasthā*) at the side of the venerable feet of the great scholar and teacher Ratnākaraśānti. After that, having gone to Vikramaśīla, [he studied] at the feet of the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitra.
For two years, he studied that treatise at his side. Then, having gone to Vikramapura, he became a monk named Maitrīgupta of the Saṃmatīya school.
Having heard the Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya, as well as the four [Tantras] up to the *Pañcakrama*.
Having performed ten million recitations of the mantra according to the tradition of Tārā, accompanied by the meaning of the four mudrās,
the Blessed One spoke in a dream: "Go to Khasarpaṇa."
Having left that monastery, he went with Khasarpaṇa and remained seated for one year.
Again, it was said to him in a dream: "Go, noble son, to the mountains Manobhaṅga and Cittaviśrāma in the Deccan; there dwells Śavareśvara."
He remains there, and he will be a benefactor to you. On that path, one named Sāgara will meet you; he is a prince residing in the kingdom of Rāṭa—go along with him as well.
Later, after you have traveled on, you will meet Sāgara at the border of the northern region, near the places called Manobhaṅga and Cittaviśrāma.

He had not heard any news. Having gone to Śrī-Dhanya, he stayed for one year; afterwards, in the northwestern region, he began to practice the sādhana of Adhiṣṭhāna-Tārā. After one month, a dream occurred: "Go, O son of good family, to the two mountains standing in the northwestern region. In fifteen days..."

It is attained. By the word of the Goddess (Bhaṭṭārikā), he goes toward the northern direction along with the assemblies; at the limit of his arrival, he is addressed by a certain man: "On the supreme day, Manobhaṅga and Cittaviśrāma will reach the appointed time (lagna); one should dwell there in happiness."

Having heard this, Paṇḍitapāda was filled with joy. When the next day arrived, he went to that mountain and, subsisting on a diet of roots, tubers, and fruits, he performed ten maṇḍalas every day for ten days, sitting upon a seat of moral discipline in the paryaṅka posture with a one-pointed mind.
He began to observe a fast. On the seventh day, a vision appeared in a dream.
On the tenth day, he began to cut his own throat; at that very moment, there was a direct manifestation [of the deity], who granted him service. Thus it came to pass for Advayavajra.
An exposition on the *Pañcakrama*, the *Caturmudrā*, and other texts was completed over the course of twelve days;

furthermore, through further instruction, it continued for five more days. Therein, he played the lute (*vīṇā*) as an illustration of all phenomena—first the *Padmāvalī* and then the *Jñānāvalī*—by Śavareśvara.

Having given the command: "Show me the illusion of killing living beings and so forth," immediately thereafter Sāgara manifested a multitude of bodies (*kāyavyūha*). He was addressed by the feet of the Sage: "O Blessed One, why am I unable to manifest a multitude of bodies?"
Śavareśvara said:
"Because it arises from conceptual construction.
The scholar said: "In that case, what should be done? May your feet command me."
The Lord of the Śavaras said: "In this life of yours, there shall be accomplishment; perform the manifestation of the Name.

Advayavajra said: "I am incapable, O Blessed One; how shall I do it? He replied: "In this matter, you shall do it through the instruction of Vajrayoginī, and the fruit will indeed bear fruit. Having spoken these words of instruction here, the venerable master vanished.
This is neither a forest deer nor a young boar.
This Vanasundarī has a face like the full moon;
for the sake of those who seek her, the sovereign of the Śabaras stands upon the mountain slope as if fashioned by a divine creator.
The sequence of non-mental engagement (*amanasikāra*) according to the order as it was heard is completed.
As before, having fully worshipped the wheel beginning with the letter *a* and performed the yoga of the Blessed Lady, [one should proceed].

Having emerged from the Praṇava-pīṭha with his face turned outward, he goes outside the curtain (kāṇḍapaṭṭa), performs the five maṇḍalas, and offers the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Then, returning with his face toward the Praṇava-pīṭha, he draws the wheel of skillful means (upāyacakra);
having caused [the disciple] to enter from there, he expands the wheel within his own heart, [visualizing it] upon the head marked by the Lord (Nātha).
Having applied the *kavaca* with the mouth, one should perform meditation upon its heart;
filling the mouth with the mantra of the Vajra-holder one hundred and eight times, and having done so, one should repeatedly strike it with the *dāimala*.
Then, visualizing the wheel of means (*upāyacakra*) revolving exceedingly rapidly, one performs the striking upon the consecrated flower.
Having sounded the hand-drum (ḍamaru) or the bell, one should recite the mantra with solemnity. One should offer incense;

if signs such as trembling arise in the disciple, then it should be explained at that very moment, otherwise not at all. Following that, having extracted [the mantra] from the wheel, the transmission of the mantra and the lineage of gurus should be recounted.

"It must be performed" is the rule of tradition. Having this in mind, [the text says] "having as its sole object the lineage of the succession of gurus and the oral tradition. And that story must be told for the purpose of generating faith; thus, the "attraction of the disciple's knowledge" is described.

"If it is not accomplished in this life, then at the time of death, the wheel enters his mouth and dissolves into its own place within my own mouth. Following this instruction from Lūyīpāda, they went to Oḍiyāna to retrieve the *Saṃvarārṇava-tantra*. There, by the side of a Yoginī...

They remained there for four days. By means of theft, the tantra was brought [to them]. On the far bank of the river, she saw that this entire sādhana had been carried away by the wind to the presence of Vajrāṅganā.
It was heard by Kukurīpāda, Indrabhūtipāda, and Lakṣmīkarā-Viruvāpāda.
To the alms-gatherer Ḍiṅgara and the alms-gatherers.
Homage to Śrī Vajrayoginī!
First, one should prepare the articles for worship as far as possible.
Having placed the *bali* offering in front, and the vessel of liquor mixed with the five nectars to the left;

the moon is in the left hand and the sun in the right hand. By means of the sound of the light-rays from the heart, having drawn [the elements] out through the nostrils and dissolved them into the hands, one performs the purification of the hands; in those hands is the vessel of liquor.
Having covered [the vessel], one should sprinkle the mantra-bath water and the articles of worship.
Then, having formed a mandala in the shape of a triangle, in its center, there is the worship with vermilion (sindūra) combined with divine water purified according to the ritual rules;
in its absence, the seed-syllable worship is performed with flowers and other materials. Immediately thereafter—

One should recollect the threefold purity. One should contemplate oneself as a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) that is pure of the three realms. Instantly, one should visualize the Blessed Lady at the center of the navel. The recitation of speech arises from the union with the two mudrās. Immediately thereafter, having projected her forth in front, there is worship, praise, and the tasting of nectar. The portion for all elemental beings is offered to the guardians of the directions, and the remainder of the nectar is presented.
Having withdrawn the Blessed Lady from the sky...
